Country.evidence_source: The study was conducted in Accra, the capital of Ghana.

Area.evidence_source: Suicide is considered a taboo in Ghana and according to the Ghana Criminal Code (1960, Act 29), attempted suicide is a crime. Consequently, individuals who attempt suicide are subject to apprehension and prosecution, and upon conviction, are subject to criminal penalties. Suicidal behaviour is also socially and culturally proscribed in Ghana to the extent that those who engage in such behaviour are sanctioned in some sub-cultures by cleansing rituals, not only on the individual but also on the extended family (Dali, 2007; Sefa-Dedeh & Canetto, 1992). Among some ethnic groups for example, suicidal behaviour carries such strong stigma that those who kill themselves are denied a proper burial (Nukunya, 2003). In some parts of the country, the body of a person who takes his/her life is whipped before being removed (Dali, 2007). Osafo, Hjelmeland, Akotia, and Knizek (2011c) found that suicide in Ghana constitutes a social injury, particularly to the family. Consequently, there is the fear that the expectation of marriage would be dashed (Adinkrah, 2012).
